blocks.x: We're recording today. We'll put the place down. Seminar Room 2, Howard Tilton Library.
What's the date anyway, Bill? I'm not sure. The time is... December 27th.
December 27th. 1961.
And I'm completely insane. And what is your name? My name is Bill Huntington. All right. That's your full name? Edward William. Bill Huntington.
Are you named after your daddy?
Yes. I see. That's right. He was a musician too. He was a violinist. Currency violinist.
My name is Dick Alamo. What's yours?
I'm Paul Crawford.
Okay. Let's see. I want to talk about you. Do you mind giving us the date of your birth?
October 2nd, 1937. And where were you born? In New Orleans. What part? In the Calton section.
Well, what kind of music were you interested in when you were young?

Well, I heard nothing but classics until I was eight. And when I was eight, my sister introduced me to jazz. My sister was an opera singer, by the way. And she introduced me to jazz when I was about eight. Through Bunk Johnson. And my mother used to turn on the Metropolitan Opera ! But when she left the room, I'd switch over to a station that played Dixie in the afternoon. You know, the afternoon Metropolitan broadcast from New York. So that's how I became interested in jazz, basically. I was about eight then. Around that time, I was also taking painting. And I had been playing piano, but I had to give that up through economic reasons.
Did your father play around the house?
No, he didn't have time to. He was quite busy working generally. He was doing the war, you
know? Who did you listen to? Who did you remember? You said Bunk Johnson for long, or else?

Let's see. Mostly Bunk. I can't think of anybody else offhand that I really listened to. I listened to Bunk and George and basically those people. Basically the album that Bunk put out, you know, when he went to New York, the Columbia album. And that was very interesting to me. What tunes were on that? High Society. I remember High Society and I remember Snagget. Snagget was on there. And that's all I can recall right now. But I used to listen to that album over and over again. It was very stimulating. And later on, we went to a Pops concert. This is when I was about eleven. And this is when the Dukes of Dixieland had first formed their little band. And they had a guitarist with them. And I got a big kick out of this. And I decided I wanted to start playing guitar. But in some way I got sidetracked to playing banjo. And then I learned that Lawrence was in town and I started taking from Lawrence. And the arrangement was that Lawrence would come up to the house. And of course we lived out in the suburbs in Lakeview. And this old colored fella would come up to the house, you know, and with the banjo. And people began to notice that there was something slightly different about our attitude towards life and family. And Lawrence was more or less part of the family and I was more or less part of his family. We'd always have some gumbo fun. My mother's a very good cook. And we'd sit around eating and then he'd... Mostly we'd sit around and play the blues, you know. Or we'd go through this little banjo method that he had. And we'd talk. I think that the talking part of it was the most educational. And later on I began sitting in with George Lewis. And I was about twelve then. When George was playing out at Manny's. Manny's Tavern. And I began making sessions around him. I began meeting the different older musicians. Amil Barnes and people I made those records with. Charlie, gee, I can't even remember his name. What did he play? A trumpet player. Charlie Love. Charlie Love. And it was a big kick meeting Albert Plenty. That's really something. And I began to do some, uh, do some, uh, reading on the history of jazz then. And, uh, read Rudy Blush's book. And became interested in the, you know, sociological aspects of it, in a sense. And, uh, are you interested in my complete development?
Sure. Yeah, just talk. Just say anything that comes to your mind. No, I'd rather not do that. . .

Well, uh, when I was about fifteen, uh, uh, actually through the efforts of Alvin Purnell. You see, I used to sit in with George Lewis and Alvin Purnell had a thing going where he'd play passing chords. And, uh, I was told when I was a kid that I had some kind of fantastic gear. I was some kind of child prodigy or something, you see. And so, uh, I'd hear all the things he was playing. And I'd tell Lawrence, why aren't you playing the same chords Alton's playing? You know, they sound like they're fitting more into the harmonic context of what's going on, you know? I'd notice that George would play a G seventh chord, run a G seventh chord against a D seventh chord. And this was sort of an unconscious dissonance. So I began to hear all these things. And, uh, through, basically throughout him, you know, I began to, uh, realize, uh, this concept of passing chords and such. And I began to get interested in modern jazz. And, uh, I had stopped listening to classics, except, uh, with the exception of, of light opera. And, and my dad, uh, would take us to, uh, different shows that were coming down, stage shows, musical comedies. And, uh, so all this kind of amalgamation of things, I guess, kind of pushed me into modern jazz. I became interested in, uh, I should say really that the, the, uh, turning point was, uh, when I met, uh, Alden Ashforth. And came down from the Wall Islands and we had known Dizzy and Charlie Parker and his people. And I began to listen to the records that he had. And I began to switch to guitar. And at first I played tenor guitar. And, uh, uh, really I began to listen, well, I had, when I was playing banjo, I had listened a lot to Lonnie Johnson. And, uh, Eddie Lang. And then Freddie Green. It was a very natural development, you know. Then I began to listen to, to, uh, I guess Teddy Wilson and Coleman Hawkins and people of that sort. And Benny Goodman. And Christian. Christian, Christian sense of time. Then I began to realize that the, the same sense of time that, that, that guys like Bunke played with, you know, that, that same time feeling was this, actually it was the same time feeling that the modernists were playing with. But it was only, uh, only using different technical aspects of the instruments. But actually the same Negro-ed feeling, you know, was, was, uh, was there. I found it very easy to make the transition rhythmically. And actually it was a liberation in, in, in a lot of ways for me, because I'd been hearing so many things that I couldn't apply to traditional jazz. And I began to play modern jazz. I think Lawrence too instilled in me a, a lot of things that, that, uh, that, uh, brought me around to modern jazz. Uh, Lawrence was pretty disgusted with the George Lewis band in general. And he used to say that all the, all the, all the, at least 90% of the musicians around town were only trying to do things that had been done long before. And he was quite bitter about these things and his attitude towards, towards, uh, traditional jazz. This was not, this was an unconscious thing on this part. He wasn't trying to turn me away from the Warriors jazz, but he was just talking about these things and naturally they turned me away. Uh, he was quite bitter about the whole thing. And he felt he wasn't much of a musician himself. He felt that his brother had been the musician of the family, his brother and his father, Billy. And, uh, through his efforts, I think, uh, I began to see that, that possibly this music, although valid at its time, was, was, uh, losing this validity. You see. Although I realized that if something is, is truly, is truly art, that it survives. And I think this is something that all jazz musicians should realize. And I think that if jazz is to endure, this should be realized. However, I think that you do have to compose for, for the present. If you are a genuine artist, if you do feel art genuine, that you have to compose for the present. Whether you're playing jazz, whether you're composing classics, no matter what you're doing, you have to work for the present. So basically that's about, that's about what my development has been.
Who did you like when you started playing? You mentioned Bonk, and then there must have been some other musicians. You said you met a lot on the mind.

Yeah, well, Bonk, and George, and Jim, and, uh, uh, let's see. I like the way Joe Watkins, was it Watkins who was playing with? I like the way Joe Watkins played time, you know. He wasn't much of a technician, but I kind of like the way he played time with the Lewis band. And of course drag had such a hell of a pulse, you know. The sitting back of drag, sitting in front of drag, you know, was really something. And, uh, and it really, really made me so, so conscious of this, this time thing, of just being able to lay back and have the time there. And that's, that's sort of grown up with me, you know, into modern jazz. And that's why so many guys think I played with such good time. And it's because of that background that I had. Uh, this, just feeling that, that, uh, you shouldn't worry about swinging, that you swing naturally. That the time will be there, you see. That the important thing is, is to express yourself and to do, uh, to create on your instrument, to not worry about swinging, that you'll swing naturally. And that, I think, is due to efforts of people like drag and Lawrence, and sitting with the Lewis band in the background. I did it.
Well, it's more or less that Lewis band that, that were your favorite out of that era.

Yeah, well, because there was nobody else to listen to, except on records. Uh, when I played with Barnes, there were very few times when his chops were up, you know, where he'd play something that was really meaningful. When he did, you know, it would really get to me. And, uh, it was really something to listen to. And so many of the other drummers would rush and, uh, retard or have some kind of problem here or there, you know. Same thing with the other instrumentalists. And then from what Lawrence was telling me, there were very few, very fine jazz musicians in the world. Right. And had been very few fine jazz musicians. He was very conscious of the ability to, uh, discern. He was, he was very, uh, particular in his likes and dislikes. And this got to me. He didn't feel that, that, uh, everybody could play jazz, and that everybody should be playing jazz, and that what everybody was playing should necessarily be called jazz because it prescribed the certain rules. He said that there was something that, that was objective, and he didn't say it in those words. But he implied that there was something objective in jazz that you could listen for. A genuineness and, and a sort of an artistic ability, I guess you could say, that was natural. And, uh, I think Bunk had it, uh, I think Jelly Roll had it. And, uh, I don't want to drop names because right now, you know, it's not a very easy thing to do anyway. Uh, but certainly a lot of people did have it, and a lot of people didn't have it, and it's been attributed to a lot of people who didn't have it. And Lawrence said that. And that's one of the things he was very strong about.

What did he teach you in, uh, in the very fundamental technical things I'm talking about? Uh, not just, just start at the beginning, before you ever got into anything like harmony, just, how to hold your banjo and how to stroke it.

Yeah, this was very interesting. He taught me, uh, he didn't teach exactly. I sort of observed. Uh, he had a very relaxed, uh, I don't give a damn attitude towards, towards playing. No, that's, that's not the right word. Uh, you know, it's not that he didn't give a damn. He, he, he just, he just kind of, he just kind of realized that, that swinging was a very natural thing. And no amount of foot stomping and, and, uh, uh, exaggerated, uh, exaggerated activity was going to make you swing. It was a very natural thing. And I sort of observed this in him. And this got to me. And I think, I think he had the, what has been called in bop musicians, the cool attitude. I think Emile Barnes had it. The cool attitude. Uh, it's just the, a very natural thing.

Well, they were restrained and casual to me. Yeah. Look at guys like that. Yeah. I mean they weren't trying to prove anything to anybody. Right. Exactly. That's what it meant. They felt like stomping their foot, they would.

If they didn't, they wouldn't. Right. That's just what it meant. That is the cool attitude, as far as I'm concerned. Well, uh, how did you hold your banjo? Oh, just the ordinary way. On the, uh, on the right thigh. It usually crossed my leg and just the way I hold a guitar, usually put it on the right thigh. And, uh, Lawrence used to use, uh, a mute on his banjo, which sort of put it halfway between, and this is in, uh, relation to timbre, put it halfway between guitar and banjo. It had more of a legato feeling than a, uh, in this, this choppy banjo feeling, which was very rhythmic, you know? And, and the tones were sustained. And it was a very, a very pretty sound, in that sense. A very, a very, uh, smooth sound. But very rhythmic, too.
Did he hit it up towards the neck, or hit it down low, or where he was stroking?

He used to hit it sort of about in the middle of the, between the bridge and where the neck would begin. Somewhere between there, where it's about the right place to hit it, to stroke it. And they didn't use any particular kind of pick or anything. And, uh, he was playing this very simple, basically because he didn't have the technique and he knew it. Uh, but he, he just had this, this very natural, this very natural thing going, very casual thing going. And so, actually, the, the teaching amounted to, to just going through this banjo method. And then after we'd go through a few little tunes, you know, and just play blues, uh, play, uh, I, uh, I improvise on different, uh, traditional things. Then I'd sit in with Lewis's band, and that sort of thing.
I noticed he, uh, one day he'd tell me, he said he wished he could solo more than he did, but he, he, uh, just said that he never was much of a solo.
No, he realized his limitations, you know. And, uh, he made no bones about it, you know. He, uh, he, uh, just knew where he stood and he knew where others stood.
Well, how was his knowledge of harmony?

That's kind of vague to me. I don't remember. I think he had a, a kind of a sketchy knowledge, uh, theoretical knowledge. He, uh, he knew about the, uh, relative family of chords and, uh, and just, uh, just the, just the very basic knowledge, what he needed to get by, I think. Uh, it wasn't, uh, it wasn't a very, a very, a very grounded knowledge or a very formal knowledge. But he did have a knowledge of, of chordal relationships, definitely.
He was able to teach you a tune by telling you the name of the chord or by showing you? Or both. Uh, let's see now.

Well, I picked up a lot of the tunes just by sitting down and, and Lewis, Lewis would, would kick off tunes, you see. And I didn't even know the tune. Uh, and, uh, I just play, you know. Uh, and, uh, I had this air, you see. And I could, uh, catch chordal relationships and key relationships. Uh, it's relative pitch. It's having relative pitch. And I could catch these things very easily. And so I had no trouble in picking up these things because usually ninety percent of the, of the traditional things were very simple harmonically, if not melodically, you know. It's, uh, same, uh, in the same way the traditional classics are. The Baroque classics are very simple harmonically. They're very simple to hear. You know. But what the voices are doing is something else, you know. But, and the same thing in New Orleans jazz. And it was very easy to hear the harmonic progression.
So there was no problem.
I don't remember ever really going through any prescribed method of learning a tune. Would George call the key?
I don't know.

Yeah, yeah. George would usually say B flat concert, you know. We wouldn't say concert, say B flat meaning concert, naturally. And the band would just kick it off. Sometimes it'd just say this tune. And since the band had been, it just called the name of a tune, and since the band had been playing it for so long, they'd just kick it off in the right key. Sometimes, I remember Lawrence told me something, and I realized later on, sometimes Jim would go through two choruses of playing in the wrong key. And finally he realized that he'd been in the wrong key. You see. This is always pretty funny. But those are the kind of things that Lawrence didn't like, and those are the kind of things that Lawrence told me that Bunk couldn't stand when he funded the band. I think...
Didn't they call it to a melody?

No, not unconscious. No, not unconscious. Not unconscious. No, not unconscious. No, not unconscious. No, not unconscious. I'm sure. But, uh... Anyway. Well, Lawrence said that he was the only one that got along with Bunk, whether that's true or not, I don't know. Lawrence said that he was constantly acting as a go-between between Bunk and the rest of the guys in the band, and that Bunk was mostly irritable and hard to get along with, very temperamental, and felt that they were pretty poor musicians, even Baby. Yeah, I think he used to call Baby the iron foundry or something.
Didn't he care for Baby as musicians? That's what I understand.

I think Bob Matthews told me that Bunk used to call him. Oh, and by the way, Bob Matthews had a lot to do with my development, too, in terms of a transition between modern jazz and traditional jazz. Because, uh, I'd get together with him and we'd play vibes. He played, he was playing vibes at the time. And I'd play guitar and, uh, would play standards, you know, things written by Gershwin. And I'd begin to get used to, uh, listening, listening for that kind of thing, you know, that kind of, uh, impressionistic, harmonic thing as applied to jazz. And, uh, he was pretty important in development. And my ideas began to stretch out, too, then. And, of course, I began to listen to Segovia a lot. But, uh, basically that's, that's what, uh, happened when I was like. Who's Bob Matthews?
Bob Matthews?
Uh, who's, uh, I don't know who is Bob Matthews? Yeah. He was a drummer. He's from a, Decatur, George. I can tell you about him. Very interesting, very interesting guy. Very intense.
Very intense. I remember.

But I couldn't figure out what he was intense about, you know. Pretty confused, I guess. I think he wanted to play the original. Like I'll do. Yeah. I think that was his, uh, I think that was his big thing. Playing the original. Anyway, he, uh, Bob laid it, went down completely on the orange jazz. Put it down, like, as being a crude form of music, I think. With the exception of very few musicians. And, uh, he was, Mm-hm. the angriest. He was about the angriest. I got to be so mad, man. Bob was, I remember about Bob, he had some very valid musical ideas. We were supposed to get up a trio. You'll probably find this very interesting. I was supposed to play classic guitar. Bob was going to play vibes and Bill Russell was going to play violin. Now we were going to do this in nightclubs in New Orleans of all places, with beer drinkers, the various happy inebriates and unhappy inebriates. What did Bill Russell say about this? Bill Russell never found out about it, fortunately. He probably will now. He doesn't listen to this track.
That's great, you know. Shall we put a note on it, restricted to Bill Russell? Tell him

what machine... This was quite an ambition of Bob's. I shouldn't desecrate this. It was kind of sacred to me. And actually, it was a very valid idea. Kind of out of context, though, you know. That's the only choral I think I'd hit with it.
Well, I don't think Bill Russell would have fit it into this group. But I could see it fitting into the audience. Yeah, that's a change. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm.
He was able to play with a band within two weeks or something like that, wasn't he?
Yes, Arlen's very talented. There was no two ways about that. He's proven that I guess.
I mean he never got to be a professional quality, but it was just like that. It was fantastic. Who was your friend that was a drummer?

That boy later turned out, I think he's kind of an unprofessional beatnik right now. He is very talented. He painted very well. And I understand he's writing very well, but he kind of lost interest in music completely because modern jazz confused him, although he liked it very much. I think he came to the same realization that I did, that you had to play music, the music that was expressive of your time, if it was to be improvisation anyway. What's his name? His name was Charles Meriwether. Actually I was always instigating him into these things and he was kind of a reluctant partner to these things. He had a very natural talent. I remember him playing things. He had a natural feeling for the beginning of choruses, the beginning and ending of choruses. In other words a natural meter, which very few people had, even musicians. He didn't have to be seen, well this is the bridge of the tune and here you play something to introduce the bridge of the tune. He didn't have to be shown any of these things. He did all these things very naturally. And it was quite, to me I was very impressed with it. But he's very unconscious of the fact that he had this, you know, he had this thing going. And he just fell away from music completely. We used to get together a whole lot and listen to Dodds, the records Dodds made, you know, Dodds washboard things. And he was a great admirer of the trombonist. And the guy that made those things with Jelly played very well as I remember. And also Tommy Ladnier, who used to dig Tommy Ladnier a lot. And I never went through the Chicago school stage, you know, too much. I dug some of the things that were going on. But not too much. I can see it, you know, as a valid musical form, especially now. I think actually they're playing, from what I've heard of them lately, they're playing better now than they ever did. I saw a television show with Bud Freeman, Pee Wee Russell, and Bob Hackett playing bass. The only thing that was missing was Wettling. I was kind of disappointed that they had Kruper in his place. But it's very valid, very groovy. I should have liked it a lot more.
What about Bix? You never got on a Bix kick ever?

No, because I think Bix is a frustrated classical composer, much in the way Thelonious is a frustrated classical composer. These people should compose. They do develop a facility on the instrument, which is really fantastic. But nevertheless, their forte, their main thing, their facet should be composition. And they should compose. I don't see why jazz musicians are so frightened to compose. I mean, Scott Joplin seems to me set a set of important forms.
You mean larger forms, not just old part-time?

Yeah, larger forms, yeah. If your facility on the instrument, in other words, Segovia shouldn't compose because Segovia, you see, is a parallel. Segovia shouldn't compose because Segovia is the kind of musician that has this kind of facility on his instrument. But these people who seem to have problems putting down, playing, at least playing their ideas on the instruments, I think should compose. They're only cheating themselves. That seems to be a kind of logical thing. I think there's a parallel between Bix and Thelonious and a few other people.
What about yourself? What do you want to do?

I just want to extend and stretch out and try to get into everything. Everything that's valid, that I feel is valid. Composition? Yeah. I'd like to write contemporary things for guitar, basically. And I'd like to still play jazz, but only good jazz. And only people. I only want jazz musicians around me to think the way I do. I feel very, you know, it's very important to me right now.
Are there enough of them around here for you to play with? Or do you feel like you're going to have to move on to another time?

No, I've got to move on. Right now I'm just gathering my things together. I was in Toronto last summer and it was very enjoyable, but I had to leave economic circumstances. They're in my control. But there's a scene there going where there's these interactions between the arts, you know, in general. And it seems to help jazz and it seems to help classical music. In other words, all art seems to benefit from it in general.
What places can you move on to? I mean what places would you consider?

Well Los Angeles and New York I guess are the only two alternatives. But when I do go I want to have a crystallization of a gathering together of the things I've been thinking about. I don't want to just go and develop up there. I want to develop here and go there. And of course further develop there. You always develop. But I do feel like I want to study for a while here before I do anything like that. Because when I do go there I want to be able to produce the things I've been thinking about and the things I'm hearing. Actually right now I'm against any kind of narrow mindedness in relation to any musical form. I think you see this narrow mindedness everywhere. Scholasticism in classical music. Muslimism in modern jazz. So on. I think this is something that's pretty dangerous.
I think the tape is about to run out so we better call it to a halt then. And they're about to close the library so thank you very much.
That's it huh?

segments.title: Opening, date, and birth in New Orleans
segments.summary: Recording details at Tilton Library, date December 27, 1961, introductions, his father a violinist, and birth on October 2, 1937 in New Orleans.

segments.title: Classical upbringing and first jazz via his sister
segments.summary: Raised on classics and opera; at eight his sister introduced him to jazz through Bunk Johnson. He also took painting and gave up piano for economic reasons.

segments.title: Bunk records, banjo lessons with Lawrence, sitting in with George Lewis
segments.summary: Listened to Bunk's Columbia album, heard the Dukes of Dixieland guitarist, took up banjo and studied with Lawrence at home, then sat in with George Lewis at Manny's and met older musicians.

segments.title: Turn to modern jazz via Alton Purnell, Alden Ashforth and Lawrence's bitterness
segments.summary: Passing chords, Alden Ashforth's records and guitar influences led him from traditional to modern jazz; Lawrence's disillusion with the Lewis band pushed him the same way; he argues jazz must compose for the present.

segments.title: Favorite Lewis band musicians and the feel of time
segments.summary: He admired Joe Watkins and Slow Drag's time and learned to swing naturally; Lawrence's strict ideas about who truly could play jazz.

segments.title: Lawrence Marrero's banjo approach and teaching
segments.summary: Lawrence's relaxed, cool attitude, muted banjo, stroking technique, simple method lessons, awareness of his limits and sketchy harmony knowledge.

segments.title: Picking up tunes in the Lewis band and keys
segments.summary: He learned tunes by ear with relative pitch while sitting in; George called keys; Jim sometimes played in the wrong key.

segments.title: Lawrence's stories of Bunk Johnson's temper
segments.summary: Lawrence said he was the go-between with Bunk, who was irritable and thought poorly of his band members.

segments.title: Bob Matthews, vibes, and the planned trio
segments.summary: Drummer and vibist Bob Matthews bridged modern and traditional jazz for him, disliked New Orleans jazz, and planned a guitar-vibes-violin trio with Bill Russell.

segments.title: Drummer friend Charles Meriwether and Chicago-style records
segments.summary: Talk of a talented drummer friend, Charles Meriwether, who quit music; listening to Dodds and Ladnier records and a television show with Bud Freeman and Pee Wee Russell.

segments.title: Bix and Thelonious as frustrated composers
segments.summary: He argues Bix and Monk should compose larger forms, citing Scott Joplin and contrasting Segovia.

segments.title: Future plans: composing for guitar and moving on from New Orleans
segments.summary: He wants to write for guitar, play only good jazz, move to Los Angeles or New York after more study, and opposes narrow-mindedness; mentions Toronto last summer.

segments.title: Closing the tape
segments.summary: The tape is running out and the library is closing.
